This superb @RealAlpineMacro chart, titled "The French Disease," shows just how gigantic the gap is that AI has to close.

France is an aging, uncompetitive, highly indebted, and politically polarized nation, where government spending accounts for a whopping 58% of GDP.

Meanwhile, productivity growth, arguably the only painless way out of mounting government debt and persistent budget deficits, has collapsed to virtually zero.

This is another excellent illustration of France's vulnerability within the Eurozone and why expectations for AI are so high.

Can AI close the gap? Partly, surely. But the divergence between government spending and productivity growth has become so extreme that additional measures will almost certainly be needed to prevent a debt crisis. If not now, then later.

I think most investors recognize these risks. But recognizing them is one thing. Actually adjusting your portfolio is another.

posts.text:
BRENT is near $110 and the supply shortage story is losing its grip. Gulf crude exports are back to 80 to 98% of pre-war levels. The barrels are flowing. The premium is fear 🛢️

JPMorgan puts Middle East exports at 17.5 million bpd, about 98% of pre-war. Kpler has Hormuz at 12 million bpd, roughly 80%. Goldman estimates 22 to 23 million bpd. TankerTrackers shows Saudi volumes 10% above pre-war.

@robin_j_brooks  explained the mechanism really well and I have to agree with him. The Baltic Dirty Tanker Index hit 7,444 on October 6, more than six times year-ago levels and the highest since 2010. The Dated Brent to front-month futures spread surpassed $50, an all-time high. Dated is near $134, futures near $107.

That $50 gap is the market paying for barrels that might not arrive. It is freight and insurance wearing an oil price costume.

Goldman's $90 December target embeds a $25 risk premium. The EIA sees $105 in Q4 falling to $84 in 2027. The far end of the curve prices the mid-$60s by the early 2030s. The market itself says the premium is temporary.

The "supply is short" story is false. The "Strait is unsafe" story is true, and it is a policy choice. IRGC attacks continued through October 17, including a supertanker mine strike. Brooks is right that the US could compress the premium. The question is whether it will.

Which breaks first: the risk premium, the IRGC attacks, or the midterm restraint?
